nodes.name: Commutative algebra
nodes.summary: Rings, modules, localization, dimension and completion. Every local statement in algebraic geometry is a statement about a ring.

nodes.name: Homological algebra
nodes.summary: Exact sequences, derived functors, spectral sequences and derived categories: the machinery that turns geometry into computable invariants.

nodes.name: Algebraic number theory
nodes.summary: Number fields, rings of integers, Dedekind domains, ramification and class groups. The arithmetic half of arithmetic geometry starts here.

nodes.name: Classical varieties
nodes.summary: Affine and projective varieties over an algebraically closed field: the Nullstellensatz, dimension, morphisms, smoothness.

nodes.name: Algebraic curves
nodes.summary: Curves and compact Riemann surfaces: divisors, genus, Riemann–Roch, maps to projective space. The case where everything can be computed.

nodes.name: Group and Galois cohomology
nodes.summary: Cohomology of profinite groups acting on modules. Measures the failure of taking Galois-fixed points to be exact; the language of local and global duality.

nodes.name: Local fields and class field theory
nodes.summary: Completions of number fields and the description of all abelian extensions by the idele class group (Artin reciprocity).

nodes.name: Schemes
nodes.summary: Spaces glued from spectra of arbitrary rings. Allows nilpotents, non-closed points and bases like Spec ℤ, so number theory becomes geometry.

nodes.name: Sheaf cohomology
nodes.summary: Cohomology of quasi-coherent sheaves: Čech computations, Serre duality, base change and semicontinuity.

nodes.name: Algebraic groups and group schemes
nodes.summary: Groups in the category of schemes: tori, reductive groups, finite flat group schemes such as μₚ and αₚ.

nodes.name: Elliptic curves
nodes.summary: Genus-one curves with a point. A group law, Mordell–Weil, reduction mod p, complex multiplication: the testing ground for every idea above.

nodes.name: Toric and tropical geometry
nodes.summary: Varieties described by polyhedral fans, and their tropical shadows. Combinatorics computes intersection numbers and degenerations.

nodes.name: Intersection theory
nodes.summary: Chow groups, Chern classes and Grothendieck–Riemann–Roch: counting how subvarieties meet.

nodes.name: Hodge theory
nodes.summary: Over ℂ, de Rham cohomology of a smooth projective variety splits into Hᵠ(X, Ωᵖ). Variations of Hodge structure track how this changes in families.

nodes.name: Étale cohomology
nodes.summary: Sheaf cohomology for the étale topology, giving ℓ-adic cohomology in any characteristic, with Galois acting on it.

nodes.name: Abelian varieties
nodes.summary: Projective group varieties: Jacobians of curves, isogenies, duality, Tate modules.

nodes.name: Modular forms and modular curves
nodes.summary: Holomorphic functions on the upper half plane with symmetry under congruence subgroups, and the curves that parametrize elliptic curves with level structure.

nodes.name: Moduli and stacks
nodes.summary: Spaces that parametrize geometric objects. When objects have automorphisms, the moduli space has to be a stack.

nodes.name: Rigid and adic spaces
nodes.summary: Analytic geometry over non-archimedean fields such as ℚₚ, where the naive topology is totally disconnected.

nodes.name: p-adic Hodge theory
nodes.summary: Studies p-adic representations of Gal(Q̄ₚ/ℚₚ) with Fontaine’s period rings (crystalline, semistable, de Rham), and compares étale, de Rham and crystalline cohomology.

nodes.name: Weil conjectures and ℓ-adic representations
nodes.summary: Zeta functions of varieties over finite fields, proved via ℓ-adic cohomology, and the Galois representations that étale cohomology produces.

nodes.name: Rational points and heights
nodes.summary: Which equations have rational solutions, and how many: Mordell–Weil, heights, Faltings, the Brauer–Manin obstruction.

nodes.name: Iwasawa theory
nodes.summary: Class groups and Selmer groups studied all at once up a ℤₚ-tower of fields; the main conjecture links them to p-adic L-functions.

nodes.name: Derived algebraic geometry
nodes.summary: Replaces rings by derived or spectral rings, so that intersections and moduli spaces carry their correct higher structure.

nodes.name: Perfectoid, prismatic and condensed
nodes.summary: Tilting passes between characteristic 0 and characteristic p; prisms unify p-adic cohomologies; condensed mathematics replaces topological spaces by sheaves on profinite sets, so that topological algebra behaves algebraically.

nodes.name: The Fargues–Fontaine curve
nodes.summary: A "curve" over ℚₚ whose vector bundles encode p-adic Hodge theory, and the stage for the geometrization of local Langlands.

nodes.name: Shimura varieties, motives and Langlands
nodes.summary: The conjectural dictionary between automorphic forms and Galois representations, and the spaces (Shimura varieties) and objects (motives) that realise it.

nodes.name: Fermat's Last Theorem
nodes.summary: Wiles and Taylor–Wiles: semistable elliptic curves over ℚ are modular, so the Frey curve cannot exist. A meeting point of most of this map.

edges.why: Varieties are recovered from their coordinate rings; the Nullstellensatz is the bridge.
A scheme is glued from Spec of rings; localization becomes restriction to open sets.
Rings of integers are Dedekind domains, where ideals factor uniquely.
Sheaf cohomology is the derived functor of global sections, computed with spectral sequences.
Group cohomology is Ext over the group ring.
Derived categories and ∞-categories become the basic objects instead of a tool.
Completing at primes gives local fields; ideles assemble them into a global object.
Non-archimedean fields like ℚₚ need their own analytic geometry.
Class field theory can be proved through the Tate cohomology of local and global fields.
Galois representations are studied through their cohomology: Selmer groups and deformation theory.
Curves are the one-dimensional varieties, where the genus controls much of the geometry.
Schemes add nilpotents, generic points and arithmetic bases such as Spec ℤ.
Toric varieties are varieties whose geometry is read off from polyhedral fans.
Elliptic curves are curves of genus one with a chosen point, and carry a group law.
Modular curves parametrize elliptic curves with level structure.
Once a point is chosen, a curve of genus g ≥ 1 embeds in its Jacobian, a g-dimensional abelian variety.
Iwasawa theory follows class groups up a tower of cyclotomic fields.
Class field theory is the GL₁ case of the Langlands correspondence.
Local class field theory describes the abelian part of Gal(Q̄ₚ/ℚₚ); p-adic Hodge theory studies the rest.
Quasi-coherent sheaves on schemes carry the cohomology that measures global obstructions.
Group schemes are groups in the category of schemes, including non-reduced ones like μₚ in characteristic p.
Étale morphisms play the role of local isomorphisms and define a new topology.
Moduli problems with automorphisms force the passage from schemes to stacks.
Integral models over Spec ℤ turn reduction mod p into geometry.
Chern classes and Riemann–Roch connect cohomology to intersection numbers.
Over ℂ the Hodge decomposition splits de Rham cohomology into sheaf cohomology groups Hᵠ(Ωᵖ).
Étale cohomology is sheaf cohomology for the étale topology.
Abelian varieties are the proper connected group varieties.
Shimura varieties are built from reductive groups; Langlands uses the dual group.
Elliptic curves are exactly the one-dimensional abelian varieties.
Modularity: every elliptic curve over ℚ is a quotient of the Jacobian of a modular curve.
Mordell–Weil: E(ℚ) is finitely generated, proved with heights and descent.
Chow groups and correspondences are the raw material of motives.
On toric varieties, intersection numbers become volumes and lattice-point counts.
p-adic Hodge theory builds p-adic analogues of the Hodge decomposition and the de Rham theorem.
Hodge structures describe the complex points of Shimura varieties and are one realisation of a motive.
Deligne proved the Riemann hypothesis over finite fields with ℓ-adic cohomology; Galois acts on Hⁱ.
Comparison theorems relate p-adic étale cohomology to de Rham and crystalline cohomology.
Faltings used abelian varieties to show curves of genus ≥ 2 have finitely many rational points.
Moduli of abelian varieties are the basic Shimura varieties.
Wiles proved semistable elliptic curves over ℚ are modular.
Modular forms are automorphic forms for GL₂.
Galois representations of modular forms and deformation rings (R = T) carry the proof.
When ℓ = p the Galois representations are far richer; Fontaine’s period rings single out the crystalline, semistable and de Rham ones.
Langlands predicts which ℓ-adic representations come from automorphic forms.
Perfectoid tilting moves p-adic Hodge theory questions to characteristic p.
Weakly admissible implies admissible becomes a statement about vector bundles on the curve.
Local conditions at p in the modularity proof are p-adic Hodge theoretic.
p-adic L-functions and Selmer groups use p-adic Hodge theory to define their local conditions.
Perfectoid spaces are adic spaces locally modelled on perfectoid algebras, where Frobenius is surjective modulo p.
Derived moduli stacks carry virtual fundamental classes and the correct deformation theory.
Moduli stacks of G-bundles and of shtukas are where the geometric and function-field Langlands programs take place.
The Fargues–Fontaine curve is built from perfectoid fields.
Fargues–Scholze geometrize the local Langlands correspondence on the stack Bun_G of the curve.
Fermat’s equation is a rational-points problem, solved by passing to elliptic curves.
